name: Water hardness vs the hard-water threshold
title: Water hardness in {city}, {SS}
alt: Chart comparing water hardness in {city}, {SS} against the threshold for hard water. {summary}

research.ask: "water_hardness_gpg" — the average hardness of water serving {city}, {SS}, in GRAINS PER GALLON as a plain number (divide ppm or mg/L by 17.1 if the published figure is in those units). First choice: the figure published by the local water utility's own annual water quality report. Second choice, only if no utility-specific figure exists: the typical hardness for this region per a named USGS or state groundwater hardness survey (e.g. the USGS groundwater hardness classification for {state}), converted to grains per gallon. Omit this field entirely rather than guessing a number with no real source behind it: a plausible-looking figure with a citation attached is worse than no figure at all.
research.source_ask: "water_hardness_source" — name the SPECIFIC published document the figure came from. For a utility-specific figure: the water utility's own annual water quality report, naming the utility and the report year. For a regional figure: the named USGS or state survey/dataset, and say plainly that it is a REGIONAL figure covering {state} rather than specific to {city} — do not word it to imply city-specific precision it does not have. Do not answer with a generic organisation name alone. If you cannot identify either a specific utility report or a named regional survey, omit water_hardness_gpg entirely.

captions: Water serving {city}, {SS} measures {self_value}; water is classified hard from {benchmark_value}. {difference} Dissolved mineral comes out of solution on heating elements and valves, so hardness decides how fast scale builds in a dishwasher, washing machine or water heater.

{city} water runs at {self_value}. {difference} Scale insulates a heating element, so it runs hotter and longer for the same result — the ordinary route to a burnt-out element, and the reason two identical machines can fail years apart in different towns.

{difference} At {self_value}, the supply to {city} sits against a classification threshold of {benchmark_value}. Every gallon leaves a little mineral behind in valves, seals and spray arms, and how much it leaves is set by the water rather than the machine.
_note: NOT converted to fetch. The USGS/EPA Water Quality Portal does return hardness samples by county FIPS (1,415 for Angelina County TX), but they mix surface water and groundwater and ranged 1-614 mg/L there, so a county median is not the municipal supply figure this chart claims — that raw dataset still isn't used directly. Instead the research ask now has two tiers: a specific utility report first, and a named USGS/state REGIONAL groundwater classification second (source_ask requires the regional tier to say so explicitly, so the caption never implies city-specific precision it doesn't have). Only omits the field when neither tier produces a real citation.
